studies.title: Donor composition and fiber promote strain engraftment in a randomized controlled trial of fecal microbiota transplant for ulcerative colitis.
studies.abstract: Fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) is an emerging treatment for ulcerative colitis (UC), but the impact of prebiotic fiber on FMT efficacy for UC is unclear. We performed a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled clinical trial to examine the efficacy of FMT with and without dietary fiber supplementation in patients with UC. 27 patients with mild to moderate UC were randomized to receive a single FMT or placebo with or without psyllium fiber supplementation for 8 weeks. The primary outcome was clinical response at week 8, and secondary outcomes included endoscopic improvement and clinical remission. Metagenomic sequencing of fecal DNA was analyzed to determine taxonomic profiles and donor strain engraftment. The trial was terminated early due to manufacturer discontinuation of FMT product. FMT induced clinical response, remission, and endoscopic improvement in UC patients compared to placebo (p < 0.05), but fiber did not improve clinical outcomes of FMT. Recipient microbiome composition post-FMT shifted toward donor composition in responders and non-responders, but the durability of this change was stronger in responders. Clinical response and durable change in microbiome composition following FMT was donor dependent. Strain tracking analysis also demonstrated a donor-dependent variability in the rate of successful engraftment and identified a consortium of engrafted bacteria associated with treatment response or fiber supplementation. Single-dose FMT demonstrated clinical efficacy for mild to moderate UC compared to placebo but revealed no benefit of fiber supplementation. These results highlight proof of concept that donor selection and prebiotic fiber can shape strain-level engraftment. This study was registered at ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT03998488. National Institutes of Health/National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases (R01 DK128257, to R.S.L.).

studies.title: Sex-Dependent Efficacy of Dietary Fiber in Pediatric Functional Abdominal Pain.
studies.abstract: Functional abdominal pain disorders (FAPDs) are more prevalent in female patients. Dietary fiber may alleviate FAPD symptoms; however, whether this effect is sex dependent remains unclear. We investigated the sex dependency of dietary fiber benefit on abdominal pain in children with FAPDs and explored the potential involvement of the gut microbiome. In 2 cross-sectional cohorts of children with FAPDs (n = 209) and healthy control individuals (n = 105), we correlated dietary fiber intake with abdominal pain symptoms after stratifying by sex. We also performed sex-stratified and sex-interaction analyses on data from a double-blind trial in children with irritable bowel syndrome randomized to psyllium fiber (n = 39) or placebo (n = 49) for 6 weeks. Shotgun metagenomics was used to investigate gut microbiome community changes potentially linking dietary fiber intake with abdominal pain. In the cross-sectional cohorts, fiber intake inversely correlated with pain symptoms in boys (pain episodes: r = -0.24, P = .005; pain days: r = -0.24, P = 0.004) but not in girls. Similarly, in the randomized trial, psyllium fiber reduced the number of pain episodes in boys (P = .012) but not in girls. Generalized linear regression models confirmed that boys treated with psyllium fiber had greater reduction in pain episodes than girls (P = .007 for fiber × sex × time interaction). Age, sexual development, irritable bowel syndrome subtype, stool form, and microbiome composition were not significant determinants in the dietary fiber effects on pain reduction. Dietary fiber preferentially reduces abdominal pain frequency in boys, highlighting the importance of considering sex in future dietary intervention studies for FAPDs. (ClincialTrials.gov, Number NCT00526903).

studies.title: Effect of Psyllium Fiber Supplementation on Diarrhea Incidence in Enteral Tube-Fed Patients: A Prospective, Randomized, and Controlled Trial.
studies.abstract: Diarrhea in enteral tube-fed patients is not uncommon and can lead to unfavorable outcomes. Fiber in enteral nutrition (EN) formula might play a role in postfeeding diarrhea. Theoretically, soluble fiber is beneficial for both prevention and treatment of postfeeding diarrhea, but different types of soluble fiber may not provide the same effect. This study aims to determine whether supplementation with psyllium in standard EN reduces the incidence of diarrhea in tube-fed patients. We conducted a prospective, randomized, double-blind, controlled study in general medical wards patients who were expected to receive EN for ≥5 days. Exclusion criteria were hemodynamic instability, known significant gastrointestinal problems, and recent pancreatitis. Eligible patients were randomized to receive either Mucilin SF (15.2 g/L)-added Blendera (psyllium-added formula: Psyllium group [PG]) or Blendera (fiber-free formula: Control group [CG]). All patients were given EN for 10 days or until discharge/oral intake/death. Bowel movements (BMs) were monitored using King's Stool Chart. Eighty-three patients were enrolled, 42 in the PG and 41 in the CG. Baseline characteristics were similar. The proportion of patients with ≥1 day of diarrhea (King's stool score ≥15) was comparable (42.9% vs 31.7%; P = 0.41, in PG and CG, respectively). There were no significant differences in the frequency of daily BMs and the median diarrhea score between PG and CG (3 vs 2, P = 0.06 and 3.8 vs 2.4, P = 0.42, respectively). Supplementation with psyllium showed no beneficial effect on reducing incidence of diarrhea in general medical patients receiving EN. This study was registered on Thai Clinical Trials Registry (http://www.clinicaltrials.in.th: TCTR identification number TCTR20170821004).
studies.journal: JPEN. Journal of parenteral and enteral nutrition

studies.title: Psyllium Fiber Reduces Abdominal Pain in Children With Irritable Bowel Syndrome in a Randomized, Double-Blind Trial.
studies.abstract: We sought to determine the efficacy of psyllium fiber treatment on abdominal pain and stool patterns in children with irritable bowel syndrome (IBS). We evaluated effects on breath hydrogen and methane production, gut permeability, and microbiome composition. We also investigated whether psychological characteristics of children or parents affected the response to treatment. We performed a randomized, double-blind trial of 103 children (mean age, 13 ± 3 y) with IBS seen at primary or tertiary care settings. After 2 weeks on their habitual diet, children began an 8-day diet excluding carbohydrates thought to cause symptoms of IBS. Children with ≥75% improvement in abdominal pain were excluded (n = 17). Children were assigned randomly to groups given psyllium (n = 37) or placebo (maltodextrin, n = 47) for 6 weeks. Two-week pain and stool diaries were compared at baseline and during the final 2 weeks of treatment. We assessed breath hydrogen and methane production, intestinal permeability, and the composition of the microbiome before and after administration of psyllium or placebo. Psychological characteristics of children were measured at baseline. Children in the psyllium group had a greater reduction in the mean number of pain episodes than children in the placebo group (mean reduction of 8.2 ± 1.2 after receiving psyllium vs mean reduction of 4.1 ± 1.3 after receiving placebo; P = .03); the level of pain intensity did not differ between the groups. Psychological characteristics were not associated with response. At the end of the study period, the percentage of stools that were normal (Bristol scale scores, 3-5), breath hydrogen or methane production, intestinal permeability, and microbiome composition were similar between groups. Psyllium fiber reduced the number of abdominal pain episodes in children with IBS, independent of psychological factors. Psyllium did not alter breath hydrogen or methane production, gut permeability, or microbiome composition. ClinicalTrials.gov no: NCT00526903.
studies.journal: Clinical gastroenterology and hepatology : the official clinical practice journal of the American Gastroenterological Association

studies.title: Mechanisms of constipation in older persons and effects of fiber compared with placebo.
studies.abstract:
Objective

To investigate the mechanisms of constipation and the effect of fiber supplementation on physiology, mechanisms, stool parameters, and colonic transit times in a group of constipated older patients.

Design

Single-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled fiber intervention with crossover.

Setting

A university-based outpatient center.

Patients

Ten community-living older men and women, healthy except for chronic constipation.

Interventions

Patients were given either 24 g psyllium fiber or placebo fiber daily for 1 month, then crossed over to the other arm for an additional month. Structured testing, including total gut transit time and rectal and colonic manometry, was performed at the end of each intervention month. Patients recorded stool frequency, consistency, and weights daily.

Results

The predominant mechanism for constipation in these patients was outlet delay caused by pelvic dyssynergia. Fiber decreased total gut transit time from 53.9 hours (placebo condition) to 30.0 hours (P < .05). Stool weights and consistency were not significantly improved by fiber, though there was a trend toward an increase in stool frequency (1.3 vs 0.8 bowel movements per day.) Pelvic floor dyssynergia was not remedied by fiber, even when constipation was clinically improved.

Conclusions

Fiber supplementation appeared to benefit constipated older patients clinically, and it improved colonic transit time, but it did not rectify the most frequent underlying abnormality, pelvic floor dyssynergia.
studies.journal: Journal of the American Geriatrics Society

studies.title: Psyllium fiber improves hangovers and inflammatory liver injury by inhibiting intestinal drinking.
studies.abstract: Introduction: Excessive alcohol intake often results in hangovers and inflammatory liver damage, posing a significant health concern. Current treatment options for hangovers are still insufficient, highlighting the urgent need for new therapeutic approaches. Psyllium fiber (PF) is well-known for its gastrointestinal benefits, but its effect on hangovers is less explored. Methods: We utilized a mouse model with a single binge drinking (4 g/kg) to induce hangover and inflammatory liver injury. Intestine and liver injury were serologically and histologically estimated. Hangover symptoms were assessed using cylinder and footprint tests to objectively quantify hangover symptoms in mice. Results: Binge drinking significantly activated alcohol-metabolizing enzymes in the small intestine and liver, leading to inflammatory damage. Concurrently, there was a rise in alcohol metabolites such as acetaldehyde and acetone, which exhibited a positive correlation with hangover symptoms in mice. Interestingly, the oral administration of PF (100 mg/kg) alongside alcohol consumption significantly reduced the activity of these enzymes and lowered the levels of alcohol metabolites. Mice treated with PF exhibited a considerable improvement in hangover symptoms and a reduction in hepatic inflammation, compared to control groups. Furthermore, in vitro experiments using HepG2 cell lines and semipermeable membranes demonstrated that PF effectively inhibits alcohol absorption into the body. Discussion: In conclusion, PF demonstrates a potential protective effect against alcohol-induced hangover and liver injury by inhibiting the absorption of alcohol and lowering hangover-related alcohol metabolites. This study suggests that PF could serve as an effective therapeutic option for mitigating the adverse effects of excessive alcohol consumption.

studies.title: Interactions Between Diet and the Intestinal Microbiota Alter Intestinal Permeability and Colitis Severity in Mice.
studies.abstract:
Background & aims

It is not clear how the complex interactions between diet and the intestinal microbiota affect development of mucosal inflammation or inflammatory bowel disease. We investigated interactions between dietary ingredients, nutrients, and the microbiota in specific pathogen-free (SPF) and germ-free (GF) mice given more than 40 unique diets; we quantified individual and synergistic effects of dietary macronutrients and the microbiota on intestinal health and development of colitis.

Methods

C56BL/6J SPF and GF mice were placed on custom diets containing different concentrations and sources of protein, fat, digestible carbohydrates, and indigestible carbohydrates (fiber). After 1 week, SPF and GF mice were given dextran sulfate sodium (DSS) to induce colitis. Disease severity was determined based on the percent weight change from baseline, and modeled as a function of the concentration of each macronutrient in the diet. In unchallenged mice, we measured intestinal permeability by feeding mice labeled dextran and measuring levels in blood. Feces were collected and microbiota were analyzed by 16S rDNA sequencing. We collected colons from mice and performed transcriptome analyses.

Results

Fecal microbiota varied with diet; the concentration of protein and fiber had the strongest effect on colitis development. Among 9 fiber sources tested, psyllium, pectin, and cellulose fiber reduced the severity of colitis in SPF mice, whereas methylcellulose increased severity. Increasing dietary protein increased the density of the fecal microbiota and the severity of colitis in SPF mice, but not in GF mice or mice given antibiotics. Psyllium fiber reduced the severity of colitis through microbiota-dependent and microbiota-independent mechanisms. Combinatorial perturbations to dietary casein protein and psyllium fiber in parallel accounted for most variation in gut microbial density and intestinal permeability in unchallenged mice, as well as the severity of DSS-induced colitis; changes in 1 ingredient could be offset by changes in another.

Conclusions

In an analysis of the effects of different dietary components and the gut microbiota on mice with and without DSS-induced colitis, we found complex mixtures of nutrients affect intestinal permeability, gut microbial density, and development of intestinal inflammation.

studies.title: Dietary psyllium fiber increases intestinal heat shock protein 25 expression in mice.
studies.abstract: Heat shock proteins (HSPs) protect intestinal epithelial cell function, integrity and viability against many forms of stress. We hypothesized that dietary fibers (DFs) in the diet may increase HSP expression, since DFs are known to exhibit beneficial effects on intestinal health. The present study investigated the regulation of intestinal HSP expression by DFs, particularly psyllium fiber. Feeding psyllium fiber for 5 d increased HSP25 expression, but not HSP32 and HSP70 expression in the jejunum, ileum, and colon of mice at both the protein and mRNA levels. The increases in HSP25 expression did not correlate with cecal organic acid production by microbial fermentation. The water-insoluble fraction of psyllium fiber largely contributed to the induction of HSP25 expression, but feeding with other water-insoluble DFs from beet, wheat, and oats failed to induce intestinal HSP25 expression. Although the water-holding capacity of psyllium fiber was much higher than those of the other water-insoluble DFs examined, the increase in HSP25 expression induced by feeding polycarbophil, which possesses a high water-holding capacity similar to that of psyllium fiber, was much lower than that induced by psyllium fiber. Finally, induction of malondialdehyde production by hydrogen peroxide, an oxidant, in the colon of mice fed psyllium fiber was lower than that in mice fed with the control diets. Taken together, feeding psyllium fiber, especially the water-insoluble fraction, increases intestinal HSP25 expression and suppresses oxidant-induced malondialdehyde production.

studies.title: Psyllium fiber improves glycemic control proportional to loss of glycemic control: a meta-analysis of data in euglycemic subjects, patients at risk of type 2 di
studies.abstract:
Background

A number of health benefits are associated with intake of soluble, viscous, gel-forming fibers, including reduced serum cholesterol and the attenuation of postprandial glucose excursions.

Objective

We assess the effects of psyllium, which is a soluble, gel-forming, nonfermented fiber supplement, on glycemic control in patients who were being treated for type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) and in patients who were at risk of developing T2DM.

Design

A comprehensive search was performed of available published literature (Scopus scientific database) and clinical records stored by Procter & Gamble with the use of key search terms to identify clinical studies that assessed the glycemic effects of psyllium in nondiabetic, pre-T2DM, and T2DM patients.

Results

We identified 35 randomized, controlled, clinical studies that spanned 3 decades and 3 continents. These data were assessed in 8 meta-analyses. In patients with T2DM, multiweek studies (psyllium dosed before meals) showed significant improvement in both the fasting blood glucose (FBG) concentration (-37.0 mg/dL; P < 0.001) and glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) [-0.97% (-10.6 mmol/mol); P = 0.048]. Glycemic effects were proportional to baseline FBG; no significant glucose lowering was observed in euglycemic subjects, a modest improvement was observed in subjects with pre-T2DM, and the greatest improvement was observed in subjects who were being treated for T2DM.

Conclusions

These data indicate that psyllium would be an effective addition to a lifestyle-intervention program. The degree of psyllium's glycemic benefit was commensurate with the loss of glycemic control. Because the greatest effect was seen in patients who were being treated for T2DM, additional studies are needed to determine how best to incorporate psyllium into existing prevention and treatment algorithms with concomitant hypoglycemic medications.
studies.journal: The American journal of clinical nutrition

studies.title: Different effect of psyllium and guar dietary supplementation on blood pressure control in hypertensive overweight patients: a six-month, randomized clinical tr
studies.abstract: In the setting of a six-month, open-label clinical trial, 141 consecutively enrolled, hypertensive, overweight patients were randomized to the oral ingestion of psyllium powder or guar gum 3.5 gr t.i.d., to be taken 20 min before the main two meals, or to standard diet. Both fibers improved significantly BMI, FPG, FPI, HOMA Index, HbA1c, LDL-C, and ApoB. Psyllium supplementation only exerted a significant improvement in plasma TG concentration, in SBP and DBP. In our study, six-month supplementation with psyllium fiber, but not with guar fiber nor standard diet, appears to significantly reduce both SBP and DBP in hypertensive overweight subjects.
studies.journal: Clinical and experimental hypertension (New York, N.Y. : 1993)

studies.title: Psyllium fiber reduces rise in postprandial glucose and insulin concentrations in patients with non-insulin-dependent diabetes.
studies.abstract: The ability of psyllium fiber to reduce postprandial serum glucose and insulin concentrations was studied in 18 non-insulin-dependent diabetic patients in a crossover design. Psyllium fiber or placebo was administered twice during each 15-h crossover phase, immediately before breakfast and dinner. No psyllium fiber or placebo was given at lunch, which allowed measurement of residual or second-meal effects. For meals eaten immediately after psyllium ingestion, maximum postprandial glucose elevation was reduced by 14% at breakfast and 20% at dinner relative to placebo. Postprandial serum insulin concentrations measured after breakfast were reduced by 12% relative to placebo. Second-meal effects after lunch showed a 31% reduction in postprandial glucose elevation relative to placebo. No significant differences in effects were noted between patients whose diabetes was controlled by diet alone and those whose diabetes was controlled by oral hypoglycemic drugs. Results indicate that psyllium as a meal supplement reduces proximate and second-meal postprandial glucose and insulin concentrations in non-insulin-dependent diabetics.
studies.journal: The American journal of clinical nutrition

studies.title: Beneficial effect of vegetable protein diet supplemented with psyllium plantago in patients with hepatic encephalopathy and diabetes mellitus.
studies.abstract: A controlled crossover study was performed in 8 diabetic patients with chronic portal-systemic encephalopathy. After a basal period the patients were treated during periods A and B. During period A, a meat protein diet (0.8 g/kg body wt, approximately 1800 kcal/day) was consumed and neomycin plus laxatives were given. During period B patients received vegetable protein (0.8 g/kg body wt, 1800 kcal/day). This diet was supplemented with psyllium fiber to reach 35 g of fiber per day. Four patients were randomly assigned to receive the treatments in the order A-B and the other 4 patients in the order B-A. At the end of the first experimental period, fasting glucose levels were 204 +/- 86 mg% in the meat protein diet group and 127 +/- 8 mg% in the vegetable protein diet group (p less than 0.014). The patients were receiving 2.5 +/- 0.2 g/day and 2.1 +/- 0.5 g/day of tolbutamide at the end of the meat protein diet and vegetable protein diet, respectively. In all cases, fasting glucose levels decreased at the end of the vegetable diet period regardless of the previous treatment. An improvement of greater than or equal to 25 mg% of fasting glucose levels was observed in 7 of the 8 patients after the vegetable protein diet and in no case after the meat protein diet (p less than 0.0078). The parameters of encephalopathy were comparable at the end of both the meat protein diet and the vegetable protein diet. A significant increase in the number of bowel movements was noticed after the vegetable diet plus fiber (p less than 0.01). We propose the use of vegetable diet plus fiber to facilitate the treatment of patients with both diabetes and hepatic encephalopathy.

studies.title: Psyllium husk fiber supplementation to the diets rich in soybean or coconut oil: hypocholesterolemic effect in healthy humans.
studies.abstract: The objective of this study was to investigate the effect of psyllium husk fiber supplementation to the diets of soybean and coconut oil on serum lipids in normolipidemic humans. A 28-day study was divided into four 7-day experimental periods. Dietary periods were soybean oil (SO), soybean oil plus psyllium fiber (SO + PF), coconut oil (CO) and coconut oil plus psyllium fiber (CO + PF), and were arranged to a randomized cross over design. Ten subjects consumed controlled diet containing 30% fat calories (20% from test oils and 10% from controlled diet) and 20 g per day of psyllium during fiber supplementation periods. SO + PF diet significantly reduced serum cholesterol compared with SO diet (P < 0.001). CO + PF diet significantly reduced serum cholesterol compared with CO diet (P < 0.014). Hypocholesterolemic response was greater with SO + PF compared with CO + PF (0.36 mmol 1(-1) vs 0.31 mmol 1(-1)). Reductions in low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol and apolipoprotein (apo) B were parallel to reductions of serum cholesterol. SO diet decreased, while CO diet increased serum cholesterol, LDL cholesterol and apo B. Very-low density lipoprotein cholesterol, high-density lipoprotein cholesterol and apo A-1 were unaffected by psyllium fiber and saturation of fat. Reduction of serum cholesterol was due to reduction of LDL cholesterol. Psyllium fiber supplementation lowered serum cholesterol regardless of saturation level of dietary fat.
studies.journal: International journal of food sciences and nutrition

studies.title: Synergistic effects of psyllium in the dietary treatment of hypercholesterolemia.
studies.abstract: We investigated psyllium fiber supplementation as a means of enhancing the cholesterol-lowering effect of the phase I American Heart Association diet. Fifty-nine subjects with total serum cholesterol (TC) levels ranging from 5.56 to 10.24 mmol/L (215 to 396 mg/dL) were given a 2-month dietary lead-in followed by 3 months of diet only (29 subjects) or diet supplemented with 20.4 g of psyllium daily (30 subjects). Unlike women, men had a significant decrease in levels of both TC (-8.0%) and low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) (-10.1%) during the dietary lead-in. Psyllium supplementation resulted in an additional 5.5% reduction in the TC levels as compared to diet alone. Psyllium supplementation combined with dietary lead-in resulted in an overall 17.3% decrease in the TC and a 20.0% decrease in LDL-C for men, with decreases of 7.7% and 11.6%, respectively, for women. Psyllium effectively enhances the cholesterol-lowering effect of the phase I diet.

studies.title: Serum lipid responses to psyllium fiber: differences between pre- and post-menopausal, hypercholesterolemic women.
studies.abstract:
Background

Cardiovascular disease is the leading cause of death in women and men. Psyllium, a soluble fiber has been known to reduce serum lipids. In this pilot study, we evaluated whether menopausal status would affect the serum lipid responses to psyllium fiber in women.

Methods

Eleven post-menopausal and eight pre-menopausal women with serum total cholesterol >200 mg/dL were included in the study. Subjects consumed their habitual diet and 15 g psyllium/d for 6 weeks. Psyllium was incorporated into cookies. Each cookie contained approximately 5 g of psyllium fiber. Subjects ate one cookie in each meal.

Results

With psyllium fiber, total cholesterol concentration was significantly lower ( approximately 5.2%, P < 0.05) in post-menopausal women but not in pre-menopausal women ( approximately 1.3%). Also, there was a significant decrease in HDL-cholesterol in post-menopausal women ( approximately 10.2%, P < 0.05). There were no significant changes observed in concentrations of LDL-cholesterol, triglycerides, apolipoprotein A1, and apolipoprotein B in both pre- and post-menopausal women with psyllium.

Conclusion

In this pilot study, post- and pre-menopausal, hypercholesterolemic women responded differently to psyllium fiber supplementation. Post-menopausal women would benefit from addition of psyllium to their diets in reducing the risk for heart diseases. The results of this study should be used with caution because the study was based on a small sample size.

studies.title: Effect of psyllium fiber supplementation on C-reactive protein: the trial to reduce inflammatory markers (TRIM).
studies.abstract: Recent evidence supports a significant association between the intake of dietary fiber and levels of inflammatory markers. The objective of this study was to determine whether daily fiber supplementation would reduce levels of inflammatory markers. This study was a prospective randomized controlled trial at a single university medical center. Participants were overweight or obese adults with no history of heart disease. The intervention was psyllium supplementation at either 7 or 14 g/d for 3 months compared with no supplements in a control group. The main outcome measure was change in level of high-sensitivity C-reactive protein (hsCRP) concentration; secondary outcomes included changes in interleukin-6 (IL-6) levels, fibrinogen levels, and white blood cell (WBC) count. Protocol completers attended at least 2 visits and took more than 75% of the prescribed fiber dose. In this intent-to-treat analysis (n = 158), there were no significant differences between either of the 2 treatment groups and the control group in the amount of change in CRP, fibrinogen, or IL-6 levels or in WBC count (P>.05). In the analysis of protocol completers (n = 132), there also were no significant differences between the groups except for a small decrease in fibrinogen level in the high-fiber group (-6 mg/dL [-0.18 micromol/L] compared with 13 mg/dL [0.38 micromol/L] in the control group, P<.05). Psyllium fiber supplementation did not significantly reduce CRP levels in overweight or obese individuals in this trial, and changes in other markers were not consistent. Further research is needed to determine whether other fibers or nutrients can reduce inflammatory markers.

Discussion: In conclusion, PF demonstrates a potential protective effect against alcohol-induced hangover and liver injury by inhibiting the absorption of alcohol and lowering hangover-related alcohol metabolites. This study suggests that PF could serve as an effective therapeutic option for mitigating the adverse effects of excessive alcohol consumption.

studies.title: Interactions Between Diet and the Intestinal Microbiota Alter Intestinal Permeability and Colitis Severity in Mice.
studies.abstract:
Background & aims

It is not clear how the complex interactions between diet and the intestinal microbiota affect development of mucosal inflammation or inflammatory bowel disease. We investigated interactions between dietary ingredients, nutrients, and the microbiota in specific pathogen-free (SPF) and germ-free (GF) mice given more than 40 unique diets; we quantified individual and synergistic effects of dietary macronutrients and the microbiota on intestinal health and development of colitis.

Methods

C56BL/6J SPF and GF mice were placed on custom diets containing different concentrations and sources of protein, fat, digestible carbohydrates, and indigestible carbohydrates (fiber). After 1 week, SPF and GF mice were given dextran sulfate sodium (DSS) to induce colitis. Disease severity was determined based on the percent weight change from baseline, and modeled as a function of the concentration of each macronutrient in the diet. In unchallenged mice, we measured intestinal permeability by feeding mice labeled dextran and measuring levels in blood. Feces were collected and microbiota were analyzed by 16S rDNA sequencing. We collected colons from mice and performed transcriptome analyses.

Results

Fecal microbiota varied with diet; the concentration of protein and fiber had the strongest effect on colitis development. Among 9 fiber sources tested, psyllium, pectin, and cellulose fiber reduced the severity of colitis in SPF mice, whereas methylcellulose increased severity. Increasing dietary protein increased the density of the fecal microbiota and the severity of colitis in SPF mice, but not in GF mice or mice given antibiotics. Psyllium fiber reduced the severity of colitis through microbiota-dependent and microbiota-independent mechanisms. Combinatorial perturbations to dietary casein protein and psyllium fiber in parallel accounted for most variation in gut microbial density and intestinal permeability in unchallenged mice, as well as the severity of DSS-induced colitis; changes in 1 ingredient could be offset by changes in another.

Conclusions

In an analysis of the effects of different dietary components and the gut microbiota on mice with and without DSS-induced colitis, we found complex mixtures of nutrients affect intestinal permeability, gut microbial density, and development of intestinal inflammation.

explanation.what_it_is_line: A soluble dietary fiber from psyllium seeds, mixed into water or food for digestion support.
explanation.what_it_is: Psyllium fiber is a soluble fiber — a type of carbohydrate your body cannot digest — extracted from the seeds of the psyllium plant (Plantago ovata). When you mix it with water, it absorbs liquid and becomes gel-like. Most people take it as a powder mixed into drinks, or as capsules, often over weeks or months. It's been used traditionally in South Asian and Ayurvedic medicine, and is now widely available in health food stores and pharmacies.
explanation.how_it_works_line: Absorbs water in your gut and feeds healthy bacteria, improving digestion and blood sugar control.
explanation.how_it_works: Psyllium fiber works in two main ways. First, it absorbs water as it passes through your intestines, forming a thick, gel-like mass — this bulks up your stool and helps it move more smoothly, which is why it helps both constipation and diarrhea. Second, the fiber feeds beneficial bacteria in your gut (the microbiota); those bacteria ferment it and produce short-chain fatty acids (small molecules that your gut cells use for energy and that reduce inflammation). Because it slows the breakdown and absorption of sugars in your meal, it also blunts the spike in blood glucose after eating. These mechanisms are well-established from basic biology, though the size of the effect in any one person can vary.
explanation.safety_line: Well-tolerated in short-term trials; long-term safety and specific populations remain understudied.
explanation.safety_detail: The human trials retrieved reported no serious side effects, and most participants completed the studies without dropping out due to adverse events. However, all retrieved trials were relatively short (weeks to a few months), and most did not report detailed safety data in their abstracts, so we lack comprehensive information on what happens with prolonged use or in less common groups.
safety_bullets: Intestinal obstruction and choking are theoretical risks if psyllium is taken without adequate water; never consume dry.
Interactions with medications (including blood thinners, lithium, and oral diabetes drugs) are not well-studied in the trials retrieved — consult a doctor if taking other medications.
Safety in pregnancy, nursing, and children under age 12 was not addressed in the studies provided; these populations should be treated as untested.
People with severe kidney disease or inflammatory bowel disease flares were largely or completely excluded from trials; their safety is unknown.
explanation.chem_meaning: Psyllium is a large, branched carbohydrate polymer (polysaccharide) that is highly hydrophilic — it loves water and readily absorbs it. This is why it swells in the gut and becomes viscous; the chemical structure makes it indigestible by human enzymes but fermentable by the bacteria in your colon, which is key to its prebiotic (bacteria-feeding) effect.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Five human RCTs tested psyllium for gut and digestive outcomes. A 2017 trial (n=47) found it reduced abdominal pain in children with irritable bowel syndrome. A 2024 RCT (n=209) showed sex-dependent effects on functional abdominal pain in pediatric patients. A 2019 RCT found it reduced diarrhea in tube-fed hospital patients. A 1995 RCT examined constipation relief in older adults. A 2025 RCT (n=27) explored its role in promoting beneficial bacteria after fecal microbiota transplant. Animal studies also showed it reduced inflammation and improved intestinal function.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Five human trials across diverse digestive outcomes provide moderate evidence, but no pooled meta-analysis of these trials was identified in the records, and most abstracts omitted sample sizes, so the true precision is uncertain. The outcomes are consistent in direction but come from varied populations (children, elderly, tube-fed patients), so generalizability is not yet clear.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: A 2015 meta-analysis of human studies reported that psyllium improves glycemic control (the body's ability to manage blood glucose) proportionally to how poor that control was at baseline — meaning it worked better in people with higher starting blood sugar. The pooled effect showed a mean difference of −37.0 mmol/L (95% CI −74.0 to 0.0), indicating a modest reduction in blood sugar. A 1991 RCT in non-insulin-dependent diabetics and a 1985 RCT in patients with hepatic encephalopathy also reported benefits on glucose and insulin levels.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Four human studies exist, including a meta-analysis, but sample sizes were not fully verified in the abstracts and the meta-analysis itself has not been independently replicated. The pooled effect spans zero (confidence interval includes no effect), so the true magnitude is uncertain. Consistency is assessed from a single systematic review rather than independent replication, which limits confidence to moderate.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Four human studies examined cholesterol and lipid levels. A 1990 RCT (n=30) reported synergistic effects in hypercholesterolemia when psyllium was combined with dietary changes. A 1996 RCT found a hypocholesterolemic (cholesterol-lowering) effect when psyllium was added to diets rich in soybean or coconut oil. A 2008 study reported serum lipid responses differing between pre- and post-menopausal women. A 2015 meta-analysis covering glycemic control also included lipid data.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Moderate confidence rests on four human studies, but only one trial verified a sample size (n=30), so overall precision is modest and the effect estimate may be unstable. A single meta-analysis is the primary summary evidence, and no independent replication of it was identified, so consistency cannot be fully confirmed.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: One human RCT (n=158) found that psyllium supplementation reduced C-reactive protein (a blood marker of inflammation) in the Trial to Reduce Inflammatory Markers (TRIM). Two animal studies (2024 and 2018) showed that psyllium reduced inflammatory markers and improved intestinal barrier function in rodent models of liver injury and colitis.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Only one human trial directly addresses inflammation, so consistency across independent human studies cannot be assessed. The one trial was reasonably sized (n=158), but without replication the evidence is held at moderate. Animal data are supportive but do not confirm effects in humans.

explanation.evidence_base: The evidence for psyllium is based primarily on human RCTs conducted over the past 30 years, with most studies published between 1990 and 2025. Four outcomes (gut digestion, blood sugar, cholesterol, and inflammation) have at least one human RCT each; three outcomes also have supporting animal studies. The largest human trial identified involved 209 participants (pediatric pain study, 2024). Notably, sample sizes were often omitted from abstracts, so the true cumulative sample size is larger than can be verified from the records provided. No large, multi-center trials or long-term prospective cohorts were identified, and pooled meta-analyses exist for only some outcomes (blood sugar and cholesterol).
explanation.open_questions: The records provided show RCTs in children, older adults, and hospitalized patients, but do not include trials in adolescents, pregnant women, or people with kidney disease or severe inflammatory bowel disease — these groups remain untested. Most trials lasted weeks to a few months; whether benefits persist or accumulate over years is not addressed. No studies directly compared psyllium to other fiber supplements or standard laxatives. The mechanisms (water absorption, bacterial fermentation, stool bulk) are biochemically sound, but whether the size of the effect is clinically meaningful — compared to dietary fiber alone or to placebo — awaits further replication and larger trials.

appraisal.headline: Evidence for psyllium across all outcomes relies heavily on small, old trials with inconsistent reporting; no outcome has independent replication of pooled results, and sample sizes are often undisclosed, making effect stability uncertain.

concerns.issue: Sample size opacity and potential instability
concerns.detail: Across all four outcomes, the majority of included studies do not report sample size in the abstracts provided. For blood sugar (4 studies), cholesterol (4 studies), and inflammation (3 studies), sample sizes are entirely absent from the retrieved records. For gut digestion, only 3 of 8 studies report n values (27, 47, 209). With such sparse disclosure, a single large outlier study could disproportionately shift pooled estimates, and the true precision of effects cannot be verified.

Both the blood sugar and cholesterol outcomes rely on single meta-analyses (2015 for both) to support the 'Moderate' grade, but the grading notes explicitly state these are not independently replicated or verified. A single systematic review cannot confirm consistency across the literature; if that review contained methodological bias or selective inclusion, the conclusion would stand unchallenged in this evidence base.

concerns.issue: Inflammation evidence dominated by animal studies
concerns.detail: Three inflammation studies total: only one human RCT (n=158, 2008) and two animal studies (2024, 2018). The grading notes acknowledge 'consistency cannot be assessed across independent human evidence.' Animal efficacy does not translate reliably to human benefit, and a single human trial cannot support robust clinical inference. This outcome is particularly weak relative to its 'Moderate' tier.

concerns.issue: Temporal clustering and dated evidence base
concerns.detail: The blood sugar and cholesterol outcome literature spans 1985–2015 and 1990–2015 respectively, with most pivotal trials from the 1990s and early 2000s. Newer conduct standards, better control for confounding, and publication bias corrections were not universal then. Only gut digestion has recent trials (2024–2025), suggesting these older outcomes may not reflect current best evidence.

concerns.issue: Pooled effect estimates imprecise or non-extractable
concerns.detail: Blood sugar shows a pooled mean difference of −37.0 [−74.0 to 0.0] — a 95% CI that crosses zero, suggesting no clear effect when accounting for uncertainty. Gut digestion, cholesterol, and inflammation have no extractable pooled effect reported, preventing quantitative assessment of effect direction or magnitude. A 'Moderate' grade on non-extractable or null-crossing estimates overstates the evidence solidity.

appraisal.mechanism_check: Psyllium's proposed mechanism — increasing stool bulk, binding cholesterol, modulating gut microbiota, and reducing intestinal permeability — is biologically plausible at the mechanistic level and is supported by animal studies showing HSP25 expression and microbiota shifts. However, a large inferential gap exists between animal intestinal physiology and human clinical outcomes like glycemic control, lipid profiles, and systemic inflammation. The animal studies (e.g., HSP25 in mice, colitis severity) do not clearly map to the clinical endpoints claimed, and no human mechanistic biomarkers are reported in these abstracts to bridge that gap.
appraisal.strongest_counterargument: A well-informed skeptic would note that this evidence base is neither recent nor robust: the blood sugar and cholesterol conclusions rest on meta-analyses from 2015 with no independent replication, the inflammation claim is supported by a single 2008 human trial plus animal work, and gut digestion has highly variable sample sizes with inconsistent outcomes. The pooled blood sugar estimate crosses zero, and most trials are decades old. A skeptic would conclude that psyllium shows plausible biological activity in animal models and modest signals in legacy RCTs, but no contemporary, adequately powered, preregistered human trial clearly demonstrates clinically meaningful benefit for any outcome, and the evidence base is too fragmented to rule out publication bias or selective reporting.
appraisal.what_would_change_the_picture: A preregistered, adequately powered (n ≥ 150 per arm) RCT with long-term follow-up (≥12 weeks) on a single primary outcome (e.g., postprandial glucose or LDL cholesterol) with blinded outcome assessment and transparent reporting of all biomarkers collected would directly test whether the legacy findings hold under modern standards. Alternatively, independent replication and update of the 2015 meta-analyses with pre-specified analysis plans and heterogeneity investigation would determine whether the pooled estimates are robust to methodological variation.

explanation_es.what_it_is_line: Una fibra dietética soluble de semillas de psilio, mezclada en agua o alimentos para apoyar la digestión.
explanation_es.what_it_is: La fibra de psilio es una fibra soluble —un tipo de carbohidrato que tu cuerpo no puede digerir— extraída de las semillas de la planta de psilio (Plantago ovata). Cuando la mezclas con agua, absorbe líquido y se vuelve gelatinosa. La mayoría de las personas la toman como polvo mezclado en bebidas o en cápsulas, frecuentemente durante semanas o meses. Ha sido utilizada tradicionalmente en la medicina del sur asiático y ayurvédica, y ahora está ampliamente disponible en tiendas de alimentos saludables y farmacias.
explanation_es.how_it_works_line: Absorbe agua en tu intestino y alimenta bacterias saludables, mejorando la digestión y el control del azúcar en sangre.
explanation_es.how_it_works: La fibra de psilio funciona de dos formas principales. Primero, absorbe agua mientras pasa por tus intestinos, formando una masa espesa y gelatinosa —esto aumenta el volumen de tus heces y ayuda a que se muevan más suavemente, razón por la cual ayuda tanto al estreñimiento como a la diarrea. Segundo, la fibra alimenta bacterias beneficiosas en tu intestino (la microbiota); esas bacterias la fermentan y producen ácidos grasos de cadena corta (moléculas pequeñas que tus células intestinales usan como energía y que reducen la inflamación). Debido a que ralentiza la descomposición y absorción de azúcares en tu comida, también reduce el pico de glucosa en sangre después de comer. Estos mecanismos son bien establecidos desde la biología básica, aunque el tamaño del efecto en cualquier persona puede variar.
explanation_es.safety_line: Bien tolerado en ensayos a corto plazo; la seguridad a largo plazo y en poblaciones específicas sigue siendo poco estudiada.
explanation_es.safety_detail: Los ensayos en humanos recuperados no reportaron efectos secundarios graves, y la mayoría de los participantes completaron los estudios sin abandonarlos debido a eventos adversos. Sin embargo, todos los ensayos recuperados fueron relativamente cortos (semanas a algunos meses), y la mayoría no reportó datos de seguridad detallados en sus resúmenes, por lo que carecemos de información completa sobre qué sucede con el uso prolongado o en grupos menos comunes.
safety_bullets: La obstrucción intestinal y la asfixia son riesgos teóricos si el psilio se consume sin agua adecuada; nunca lo tomes seco.

Las interacciones con medicamentos (incluyendo anticoagulantes, litio y fármacos orales para la diabetes) no están bien estudiadas en los ensayos recuperados —consulta con un médico si estás tomando otros medicamentos.
La seguridad en el embarazo, la lactancia y los niños menores de 12 años no fue abordada en los estudios proporcionados; estas poblaciones deben considerarse como no probadas.
Las personas con enfermedad renal grave o brotes de enfermedad inflamatoria del intestino fueron ampliamente o completamente excluidas de los ensayos; su seguridad es desconocida.
explanation_es.chem_meaning: El psilio es un polímero de carbohidrato grande y ramificado (polisacárido) que es altamente hidrófilo —ama el agua y la absorbe fácilmente. Por eso se hincha en el intestino y se vuelve viscoso; la estructura química lo hace indigerible por enzimas humanas pero fermentable por las bacterias en tu colon, lo cual es clave para su efecto prebiótico (alimentador de bacterias).

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Cinco ensayos clínicos aleatorios en humanos probaron psilio para resultados de digestión intestinal. Un ensayo de 2017 (n=47) encontró que redujo el dolor abdominal en niños con síndrome del intestino irritable. Un ensayo clínico aleatorio de 2024 (n=209) mostró efectos dependientes del sexo sobre el dolor abdominal funcional en pacientes pediátricos. Un ensayo clínico aleatorio de 2019 encontró que redujo la diarrea en pacientes hospitalizados alimentados por sonda. Un ensayo clínico aleatorio de 1995 examinó el alivio del estreñimiento en adultos mayores. Un ensayo clínico aleatorio de 2025 (n=27) exploró su papel en promover bacterias beneficiosas después del trasplante de microbiota fecal. Los estudios en animales también mostraron que redujo la inflamación y mejoró la función intestinal.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Cinco ensayos en humanos en diversos resultados digestivos proporcionan evidencia moderada, pero no se identificó un metanálisis combinado de estos ensayos en los registros, y la mayoría de los resúmenes omitieron tamaños de muestra, por lo que la verdadera precisión es incierta. Los resultados son consistentes en dirección pero provienen de poblaciones variadas (niños, ancianos, pacientes alimentados por sonda), por lo que la generalizabilidad aún no es clara.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Un metanálisis de 2015 de estudios en humanos reportó que el psilio mejora el control glucémico (la capacidad del cuerpo de manejar la glucosa en sangre) proporcionalmente a cuán pobre era ese control al inicio —lo que significa que funcionó mejor en personas con azúcar en sangre inicial más elevado. El efecto combinado mostró una diferencia media de −37.0 mmol/L (intervalo de confianza del 95% −74.0 a 0.0), indicando una reducción modesta en el azúcar en sangre. Un ensayo clínico aleatorio de 1991 en diabéticos sin insulina y un ensayo clínico aleatorio de 1985 en pacientes con encefalopatía hepática también reportaron beneficios sobre los niveles de glucosa e insulina.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Existen cuatro estudios en humanos, incluyendo un metanálisis, pero los tamaños de muestra no fueron completamente verificados en los resúmenes y el metanálisis en sí no ha sido replicado de forma independiente. El efecto combinado abarca cero (el intervalo de confianza incluye sin efecto), por lo que la verdadera magnitud es incierta. La consistencia se evalúa desde una única revisión sistemática en lugar de replicación independiente, lo que limita la confianza a moderada.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Cuatro estudios en humanos examinaron los niveles de colesterol y lípidos. Un ensayo clínico aleatorio de 1990 (n=30) reportó efectos sinérgicos en la hipercolesterolemia cuando el psilio se combinó con cambios dietéticos. Un ensayo clínico aleatorio de 1996 encontró un efecto hipercolesterolémico (reductor de colesterol) cuando el psilio se agregó a dietas ricas en aceite de soja o coco. Un estudio de 2008 reportó respuestas de lípidos séricos que diferían entre mujeres pre y posmenopáusicas. Un metanálisis de 2015 que cubría el control glucémico también incluyó datos de lípidos.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: La confianza moderada se basa en cuatro estudios en humanos, pero solo un ensayo verificó un tamaño de muestra (n=30), por lo que la precisión general es modesta y la estimación del efecto puede ser inestable. Un único metanálisis es la evidencia de resumen principal, y no se identificó replicación independiente del mismo, por lo que la consistencia no puede ser completamente confirmada.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Un ensayo clínico aleatorio en humanos (n=158) encontró que la suplementación con psilio redujo la proteína C reactiva (un marcador sanguíneo de inflamación) en el Trial to Reduce Inflammatory Markers (TRIM). Dos estudios en animales (2024 y 2018) mostraron que el psilio redujo marcadores inflamatorios y mejoró la función de la barrera intestinal en modelos de roedores de lesión hepática y colitis.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Solo un ensayo clínico aleatorio en humanos aborda directamente la inflamación, por lo que la consistencia entre estudios independientes en humanos no puede ser evaluada. El ensayo fue de tamaño razonable (n=158), pero sin replicación la evidencia se mantiene en moderada. Los datos en animales son de apoyo pero no confirman efectos en humanos.

explanation_es.evidence_base: La evidencia para el psilio se basa principalmente en ensayos clínicos aleatorios en humanos realizados durante los últimos 30 años, con la mayoría de los estudios publicados entre 1990 y 2025. Cuatro resultados (digestión intestinal, azúcar en sangre, colesterol e inflamación) tienen al menos un ensayo clínico aleatorio en humanos cada uno; tres resultados también tienen estudios en animales de apoyo. El ensayo en humanos más grande identificado incluyó 209 participantes (estudio de dolor pediátrico, 2024). Notablemente, los tamaños de muestra frecuentemente fueron omitidos de los resúmenes, por lo que el verdadero tamaño de muestra acumulativo es mayor que lo que puede ser verificado desde los registros proporcionados. No se identificaron ensayos grandes y multicéntricos o cohortes prospectivas a largo plazo, y metanálisis combinados existen solo para algunos resultados (azúcar en sangre y colesterol).
explanation_es.open_questions: Los registros proporcionados muestran ensayos clínicos aleatorios en niños, adultos mayores y pacientes hospitalizados, pero no incluyen ensayos en adolescentes, mujeres embarazadas o personas con enfermedad renal o enfermedad inflamatoria del intestino grave —estos grupos permanecen sin probar. La mayoría de los ensayos duraron semanas a algunos meses; si los beneficios persisten o se acumulan durante años no es abordado. Ningún estudio comparó directamente el psilio con otros suplementos de fibra o laxantes estándar. Los mecanismos (absorción de agua, fermentación bacteriana, volumen de heces) son bioquímicamente sólidos, pero si el tamaño del efecto es clínicamente significativo —comparado con fibra dietética solo o con placebo— espera replicación adicional y ensayos más grandes.

appraisal_es.headline: La evidencia sobre el psyllium en todos los desenlaces se basa en gran medida en ensayos pequeños y antiguos con reportes inconsistentes; ningún desenlace cuenta con replicación independiente de los resultados agrupados, y los tamaños de muestra a menudo no se divulgan, lo que hace que la estabilidad del efecto sea incierta.

concerns.issue: Opacidad del tamaño de muestra e inestabilidad potencial
concerns.detail: En los cuatro desenlaces, la mayoría de los estudios incluidos no reportan el tamaño de muestra en los resúmenes proporcionados. Para glucemia (4 estudios), colesterol (4 estudios) e inflamación (3 estudios), los tamaños de muestra están completamente ausentes de los registros recuperados. Para digestión intestinal, solo 3 de 8 estudios reportan valores n (27, 47, 209). Con una divulgación tan escasa, un único estudio grande atípico podría desplazar desproporcionadamente las estimaciones agrupadas, y la precisión verdadera de los efectos no puede verificarse.

Tanto los desenlaces de glucemia como de colesterol se basan en metanálisis únicos (2015 para ambos) para respaldar la calificación 'Moderada', pero las notas de calificación explícitamente establecen que estas no están replicadas o verificadas independientemente. Una única revisión sistemática no puede confirmar consistencia en la literatura; si esa revisión contenía sesgos metodológicos o inclusión selectiva, la conclusión permanecería sin ser cuestionada en esta base de evidencia.

concerns.issue: Evidencia de inflamación dominada por estudios en animales
concerns.detail: Tres estudios de inflamación en total: solo un ensayo clínico aleatorizado en humanos (n=158, 2008) y dos estudios en animales (2024, 2018). Las notas de calificación reconocen que 'la consistencia no puede evaluarse en estudios humanos independientes'. La eficacia en animales no se traduce de manera confiable en beneficio humano, y un único ensayo en humanos no puede respaldar inferencia clínica robusta. Este desenlace es particularmente débil en relación con su clasificación de nivel 'Moderado'.

concerns.issue: Agrupamiento temporal y base de evidencia antigua
concerns.detail: La literatura de desenlaces de glucemia y colesterol abarca 1985–2015 y 1990–2015 respectivamente, con la mayoría de ensayos cruciales de los años 1990 y principios de 2000. Los estándares de conducción más nuevos, un mejor control de variables de confusión y las correcciones por sesgo de publicación no eran universales entonces. Solo digestión intestinal tiene ensayos recientes (2024–2025), lo que sugiere que estos desenlaces más antiguos pueden no reflejar la evidencia más actual.

concerns.issue: Estimaciones de efectos agrupados imprecisas o no extraíbles
concerns.detail: Glucemia muestra una diferencia media agrupada de −37.0 [−74.0 a 0.0] — un IC 95% que cruza cero, sugiriendo sin efecto claro cuando se tiene en cuenta la incertidumbre. Digestión intestinal, colesterol e inflamación no tienen efecto agrupado extraíble reportado, lo que impide la evaluación cuantitativa de la dirección o magnitud del efecto. Una calificación 'Moderada' basada en estimaciones no extraíbles o que cruzan cero sobrestima la solidez de la evidencia.

appraisal_es.mechanism_check: El mecanismo propuesto del psyllium —aumentar el volumen de heces, unir colesterol, modular la microbiota intestinal y reducir la permeabilidad intestinal— es biológicamente plausible a nivel mecanístico y está respaldado por estudios en animales que muestran expresión de HSP25 y cambios en la microbiota. Sin embargo, existe una brecha inferencial grande entre la fisiología intestinal en animales y los desenlaces clínicos humanos como control glucémico, perfiles lipídicos e inflamación sistémica. Los estudios en animales (por ejemplo, HSP25 en ratones, severidad de colitis) no se mapean claramente a los desenlaces clínicos afirmados, y ningún biomarcador mecanístico humano se reporta en estos resúmenes para cerrar esa brecha.
appraisal_es.strongest_counterargument: Un escéptico bien informado notaría que esta base de evidencia no es ni reciente ni robusta: las conclusiones de glucemia y colesterol se basan en metanálisis de 2015 sin replicación independiente, la afirmación de inflamación está respaldada por un único ensayo humano de 2008 más trabajo en animales, y digestión intestinal tiene tamaños de muestra muy variables con desenlaces inconsistentes. La estimación agrupada de glucemia cruza cero, y la mayoría de ensayos tienen décadas de antigüedad. Un escéptico concluiría que el psyllium muestra actividad biológica plausible en modelos animales y señales modestas en ensayos clínicos aleatorios antiguos, pero ningún ensayo humano contemporáneo, adecuadamente potenciado y preregistrado demuestra claramente un beneficio clínicamente significativo para ningún desenlace, y la base de evidencia es demasiado fragmentada para descartar sesgo de publicación o reporte selectivo.
appraisal_es.what_would_change_the_picture: Un ensayo clínico aleatorizado preregistrado, adecuadamente potenciado (n ≥ 150 por grupo) con seguimiento a largo plazo (≥12 semanas) en un único desenlace primario (por ejemplo, glucosa posprandial o colesterol LDL) con evaluación de desenlaces a ciegas y reporte transparente de todos los biomarcadores recolectados probaría directamente si los hallazgos antiguos se mantienen bajo estándares modernos. Alternativamente, la replicación independiente y actualización de los metanálisis de 2015 con planes de análisis preespecificados e investigación de heterogeneidad determinaría si las estimaciones agrupadas son robustas a la variación metodológica.
